hook: Two thousand years ago, on the last night of October, entire villages lit giant fires, pulled on terrifying masks, and set food outside their doors. It looked like a party. It wasn't.

scenes.text: This is the true story of Halloween. And the real history is darker than any horror movie ever made. Because everything you do tonight — the costumes, the candy, the carved pumpkins — was invented by people who were genuinely afraid of the dark.

scenes.text: Our story begins in ancient Ireland, two thousand years ago, with the Celts. Their year didn't begin in January. It began on the first of November — the day winter started. And the night before it had a name: Samhain. Summer's end.

scenes.text: For the Celts, winter wasn't a season. It was an enemy. Crops died. Livestock starved. The cold killed the old and the weak. And on Samhain night, they believed something worse than the cold was walking the earth.

scenes.imagePrompt: A moonlit Celtic field at night, translucent ghostly figures rising from the ground and drifting toward a distant village, full moon behind clouds.
scenes.text: They believed the veil between the world of the living and the world of the dead grew thin on this one night — thin enough for spirits to cross. The souls of everyone who had died that year were coming home. And not all of them were friendly.

scenes.text: So the Celts fought back the only way they knew how. They built enormous sacred bonfires on the hilltops — walls of flame meant to hold the darkness back. Every family carried fire home from those bonfires to relight their hearth for the winter.

scenes.text: Then came the masks. The Celts pulled on animal heads and skins — stags, wolves, boars — and smeared themselves with ash from the sacred fires. The idea was simple and desperate: if you looked like a monster, the real monsters might leave you alone.

scenes.text: They left food and drink outside their doors — offerings for the wandering dead. A hungry ghost, they reasoned, was a dangerous ghost. Feed it, and maybe it would pass your house by. Refuse it, and you might not live to see the spring.

scenes.text: The night belonged to fortune-tellers, too. The Druids, the Celtic priests, believed the thin veil let them see the future — who would marry, who would die, whether the harvest would survive. And people were frightened enough to believe them.

scenes.text: Then the Romans arrived. When they conquered the Celtic lands, they didn't destroy Samhain. They absorbed it, the way Rome absorbed everything. Two of their own festivals melted straight into the night of the dead.

scenes.text: The first was Feralia, a Roman day for honoring the dead. The second honored Pomona, the goddess of fruit and orchards — and her symbol was the apple. That's why, two thousand years later, you're still bobbing for apples on Halloween night.

scenes.text: Rome brought roads, laws, and order to the Celtic world. But October thirty-first stayed wild. You can conquer a people. It's much harder to conquer the night they're most afraid of.

scenes.text: Centuries later, the Christian Church tried a different strategy. If you can't beat the festival, baptize it. In the seven hundreds, Pope Gregory the Third moved All Saints' Day — a feast honoring every saint — to the first of November.

scenes.text: The night before became All Hallows' Eve. Say it fast, let a few centuries chew on it, and you get Halloween. The Church had claimed the date. But the people kept the bonfires, the masks, and the ghosts.
